extracted.intended_audience: general readers, writers, students and scholars interested in science fiction (genre overview and craft)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative dimensions for creating or assessing science fiction works, covering subgenre alignment, worldbuilding, narrative craft, scientific plausibility, themes, and community reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard vs. soft science fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which a work emphasizes scientific/technical rigor (hard) versus social, political or character-driven concerns (soft).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page references the 'Hard Versus Soft Science Fiction' debate and collections of authors weighing in; use of technical detail and respect for scientific plausibility characterise 'hard' SF, while 'soft' SF privileges ideas, social consequences and character. Consider where a story sits on this spectrum when evaluating plausibility and focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subgenre suitability and conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Conformity to and effective use of subgenre conventions (e.g., space opera, cyberpunk, steampunk, cli‑fi, military, utopian/dystopian, kaiju, biopunk, solarpunk, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article enumerates many subgenres; assess whether the work meets reader expectations for its chosen subgenre (tone, typical themes, tropes) or knowingly subverts them. Subgenre alignment affects plot devices, technology, setting, and thematic focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worldbuilding and setting plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Construction of the fictional world (alternate history, planets, societies, technologies) and its internal consistency and believability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worldbuilding should sustain suspension of disbelief via coherent rules, believable institutions and consequences of technologies. The page lists worldbuilding under 'Setting' and related topics (terraforming, Dyson sphere, space stations), implying importance of imaginative yet internally consistent detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sense of wonder
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability of the story to evoke awe, curiosity or big‑idea amazement — a traditional aim of much science fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentioned as a key element of speculative fiction; evaluate whether the narrative elicits a lasting emotional or intellectual response through imaginative scale, novel concepts or spectacular revelations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and accuracy of science/technology
rubrics_metrics.description: How the work uses scientific ideas and technologies — whether as rigorously developed speculative extrapolation, plausible background, or merely as plot device (rubber science).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page cites examples of SF predicting technologies (Jetsons, Wells) and references works on using medicine in SF. Check whether scientific premises are coherent within the story, whether technical detail serves theme/plot, and whether errors undermine credibility when accuracy is expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theme and idea development
rubrics_metrics.description: Depth and clarity in exploring central themes (e.g., utopia/dystopia, transhumanism, AI, climate/clifi, colonialism, ethics of technology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Science fiction often interrogates social, political or philosophical questions. Evaluate how well the narrative engages with its themes, whether ideas are interrogated rather than merely illustrated, and whether thematic complexity enhances the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization and character arc
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality of characters (protagonist, antagonist, supporting cast), their development, motivations, and emotional complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'Narrative' section lists many character concepts (character arc, foil, confidant, tragic hero). Assess believable motivations, growth/change across the story, and how characters embody or challenge thematic concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot, structure and pacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Organization of events, narrative drive, management of conflict, use of plot devices (foreshadowing, Chekhov's gun, twists), and overall pacing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page's narrative glossary includes conflict, cliffhanger, foreshadowing, Chekhov's gun, plot twist and pace; evaluate coherence of plot logic, effective escalation of stakes, and rhythm appropriate to the story's scope (short story vs novel).

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative techniques and point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice and handling of narration (first/third person, omniscient, unreliable narrator, multiple narrators, tense) and its effect on reader engagement and information control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article lists narration elements (first-/second-/third-person, unreliable narrator, stream of consciousness). Assess whether POV choices serve suspense, theme, empathy, and clarity, and whether shifts are handled smoothly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style, language and voice (including 'show, don't tell')
rubrics_metrics.description: Prose quality: diction, imagery, tone, voice, and use of the craft maxim 'show, don't tell'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under 'Style' the page includes 'Show, don't tell', diction and imagery. Evaluate vividness, economy, appropriateness of register, and whether descriptive choices enhance rather than obstruct speculative ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of tropes and originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Use, inversion or subversion of genre tropes (e.g., alien invasion, AI takeover, galactic empire) and the work's originality relative to established patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article's lists of common themes/tropes imply that originality can come from fresh angles, character focus, worldbuilding twists or thematic recontextualization; beware reliance on clichés without new insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical, cultural and social awareness (representation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treatment of race, gender, culture, and social power within speculative settings — sensitivity and complexity in portrayal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page references debates (e.g., sexism in publishing, political controversies around awards) and regional/identity subgenres (Afrofuturism, Africanfuturism). Evaluate whether the work thoughtfully engages diverse perspectives and avoids harmful stereotyping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific/medical plausibility when central (use of specialist knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriate use of specialist fields (medicine, biology, engineering) when they are central to plot or theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites 'Using Medicine in Science Fiction' as a writer's guide; when medical/biological detail is pivotal, accuracy or believable extrapolation strengthens the work, and glaring errors can undermine credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and genre‑appropriate humor (e.g., comedy SF)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consistency and effectiveness of tone, including comedic approaches when the subgenre calls for it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page lists 'Comedy Science Fiction' as a subcategory; assess timing, satire, and whether humor supports rather than undercuts worldbuilding or stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community reception and recognition (fandom, awards, conventions)
rubrics_metrics.description: How a work is received by fan communities, critics, and awards bodies (Hugo, Nebula, etc.) as one measure of impact or quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article details fanzines, conventions and awards lists; while reception is not a craft metric per se, award nominations, critical discussion and fandom engagement are relevant indicators of cultural impact and resonance.
